title: SYSK Selects: How the MPAA Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the June episode on how the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) works. Josh introduces it as a pick tied to his Movie Crush show. The hosts trace the MPAA's origins and the Hays Code, the 1968-era creation of the G/PG/R/X ratings and the PG-13 rating after Spielberg's Indiana Jones and Gremlins, the NC-17 replacement for X, and the secret Classification and Ratings Administration (CARA) raters and appeals process, as exposed by Kirby Dick's documentary This Film Is Not Yet Rated. They also cover the MPAA's lobbying against piracy and VCRs, the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, the inconsistent treatment of sex and violence, and the closing listener mail about wild parrots of San Francisco.
topics: This Film Is Not Yet Rated

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Selects episode, explaining he picked the MPAA episode because of his Movie Crush show. Chuck and Josh banter about the MPAA and ratings, and Chuck says he has no problem with ratings in principle but objects to how the MPAA does it.

segments.title: Origin of PG-13
segments.summary: The hosts explain PG-13 was created after Steven Spielberg's Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and Gremlins were rated PG despite their intensity. The rating filled the gap between PG and R, and PG-13 is now the rating most likely to earn box office money. Filmmakers aim for it, sometimes by adding violence.
topics: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom

segments.title: Hays Code and early Hollywood censorship
segments.summary: The MPAA was founded in the early 1920s when local authorities controlled moral stamps on films. Will Hays, its first president, installed the Hays Code, a strict set of rules, to head off local obscenity laws that threatened business. The hosts describe the code's content rules for 1930s and 1940s films.

segments.title: Breakdown of the Hays Code and the Ginzburg case
segments.summary: After World War Two, the Hays Code loosened, with The Man with the Golden Arm cited as an example. By the late 1950s it was effectively dead. A Supreme Court obscenity case involving a New York store owner named Ginzburg shifted control toward local municipalities, prompting Jack Valenti to create a self-policing rating system.
topics: The Man with the Golden Arm

segments.title: Original G-PG-R-X ratings and the NC-17 replacement
segments.summary: The original ratings were G, PG, R and X, with X used as a marketing tool. The hosts describe the meanings of G, PG, PG-13, R and NC-17 as of 2014. NC-17 replaced X, and Henry & June was the first film to receive it, which hurt its commercial prospects.

segments.title: How CARA ratings work and secrecy
segments.summary: CARA, the MPAA's ratings arm, uses raters who watch films and vote on a rating, then a senior rater explains it to the filmmaker. The ratings are voluntary in law but theaters require them, and submission costs a fee. Raters are supposedly unaffiliated parents, but the process is secret and unaccountable. Kirby Dick's documentary This Film Is Not Yet Rated exposed the raters' identities and the appeals process.
topics: This Film Is Not Yet Rated

segments.title: MPAA lobbying, piracy and digital distribution
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the MPAA's power as a lobbying group for six major studios and the threat digital distribution poses to its rating-based leverage. They cover its history of opposing VCRs, its role in passing the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, and camcording and screener piracy.

segments.title: Inconsistent ratings: sex, violence and check the box
segments.summary: The hosts criticize the MPAA for treating sex and LGBT content more harshly than violence, citing examples such as Blue Is the Warmest Color, A Longtime Companion, Afternoon Delight, Rushmore and Todd Solondz's refusal to cut. They also discuss the Check the Box descriptions and marketing to minors.

segments.title: Closing thoughts and documentary recommendation
segments.summary: The hosts urge listeners to research the MPAA, recommend This Film Is Not Yet Rated, and note the MPAA's conflict-of-interest critiques and the Chris Dodd era. They point listeners to the How Stuff Works site for more.

segments.title: Listener mail: wild parrots of San Francisco
segments.summary: A listener named Amy describes the wild parrots of San Francisco, which now roost near her aunt's home in Brisbane, and recommends the documentary The Wild Parrots of Telegraph Hill.
topics: The Wild Parrots of Telegraph Hill
